title: Emerging Markets-Bond issues testify to risk appetite; stx soar
text:
LONDON, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Emerging equities posted a record high for the fourth straight session on Thursday as expectations grew of another U.S. interest rate cut while a successful Turkish Eurobond sale testified to abundant investor appetite for risk.   

U.S. housing and employment data later in the day are widely seen as making the case for more policy easing even though high-yield assets are basking in the afterglow of last week's 50 basis point rate cut by the Federal Reserve. The yen fell back, indicating rising interest in carry trades.   

Emerging equities on the  Morgan Stanley benchmark index rose 1.5 percent to a new high, just short of 1200 points <.MSCIEF>. The index has gained over 30 percent so far this year, compared with 12 percent gains for the MSCI World index <.MIWD00000PUS>.   

Bond markets were likewise buoyant, with yield spreads on  JP Morgan's EMBI Plus index contracting 4 basis points to 194 bps over U.S. Treasuries. Turkey's portion of the EMBI Plus tightened 2 bps to 211 bps over U.S. Treasuries.   

"There is appetite for sovereigns," said Kaushik Rudra, emerging debt strategist at  Lehman Brothers. "People are differentiating between corporates and sovereigns and have more confidence in the sovereign outlook than the corporate outlook."   

This view was confirmed by news that the order book for Ghana's debut $750 million Eurobond had come in at almost $3 billion. The deal will price later in the day and yield guidance on the bond has tightened to 8.5 percent, a market source said.   

The Turkey deal came with a bit of a concession to the curve, analysts said, noting it was 5-7 bps wider to the curve and about 4 bps wider than the existing 2010 issue.   

Bond traders said the yield on the issue had initially snapped in 10 bps on Thursday before rising back.   

"Most of the activity this morning has been in the Turkey '18s but the rest of EM is mostly quiet and trading cautiously ahead of the U.S. data releases, and given the strength we witnessed yesterday," Commerzbank trader Paul Timmons said.   

STILL SOME STRESS   

Rudra said investors were still cautious, reflected in the fact that credits less dependant on financial markets are outperforming. There is also some rotation of cash into the more liquid assets from the less liquid, he said.   

"The tone of the market is better. More risk is being put on but these two trends are definitely there within that -- a bit of differentiation and seeking of liquidity."   

The stresses manifested themselves in Russian money market rates which had soared to two-year highs around 10 percent on Wednesday. They eased to 8 percent on Thursday and the central bank injected 48 billion roubles ($2 billion) after putting in about 64 billion roubles in total on Wednesday.   

Kazakhstan's central bank also delayed a rise in banks' reserve requirements to Jan. 15, 2008 from the previously planned Oct. 9. to smooth the liquidity squeeze on local markets.   

On currencies, South Africa's rand rose to a new 2-month high versus the dollar <ZAR=>, helped by gold prices near a 28-year high and platinum near a 10-month peak. It broke past the key resistance level of 6.93 and is now testing 6.88 per dollar.   

The lira hit a new six-year high <TRY=>, the best performing emerging currency this year with gains of 16.4 percent.   

The Czech crown was flat as the central bank held interest rates steady as expected.   

Some of the upward pressure on the Saudi riyal subsided as the central bank reiterated its commitment to its dollar peg. But the riyal remains at 3.74 per dollar, above the peg level of 3.75.   

"Overall, the market hasn't been shaken and remains positive that the riyal peg will go,"  BNP Paribas said in a note.   

"We continue to believe that Saudi Arabia could indeed intervene in the short term should 1-year forwards move below 300 pips but over the medium term we continue to believe that currency regime change is increasingly inevitable." [20070927 104715 GMT]

title: Saudi riyal stable,no devaluation seen now-dealers.
text:
DUBAI, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The Saudi Arabian riyal, under the gun from slumping oil prices, is not in any immediate danger of devaluation despite reports of central bank intervention in the market, dealers and analysts said on Sunday. 

 "I'm not expecting any more intervention activity for the time being...and certainly not today," one Riyadh-based dealer told Reuters. 

 "There is no sign of devaluation on the horizon and I don't see any reason why they (the central bank) would default in the near future," he added. 

 The kingdom, which draws around three-quarters of its revenues from oil, has seen its economy hit hard by the decline in world oil prices over the past year. 

 The Financial Times reported on Friday that this had resulted in a spate of heavy intervention by the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency (SAMA) or central bank in the currency markets on Thursday, with pressure mounting on the riyal. 

 But dealers said although there had been signs of some intervention in the market last week, activity had now returned to normal. 

 "It looks like the central bank has everything under control and trading is as normal today," another dealer said. 

 The riyal normally trades in a narrow band around its peg of 3.7500 to the dollar. The dollar is the medium for pricing oil and so accounts for most Saudi exports. The kingdom is by far the world's largest oil producer and exporter. 

 By 1145 GMT the riyal was quoted at 3.7505/15 to the dollar. 

 SAMA on Saturday denied reports it had been forced to intervene to defend the currency against speculators. 

 The central bank said it had not intervened and had no intention of changing the riyal's exchange rate. 

 "The statement from SAMA saying that they did not see any reason why they should devalue the currency was very forthright and I firmly believe that the Saudi riyal will maintain its parity," said Badar Kazmi, regional head of treasury at Standard Chartered in Dubai. 

 Last August the riyal came under attack from foreign-based speculators who were betting on a devaluation as oil prices slumped. 

 Government sources said SAMA pumped $750 million into the market to shield the riyal on that occasion. 

 The Saudi government traditionally defends its currency through intervention rather than by increasing interest rates. Saudi Arabia last devalued its currency in 1986. 

 Diplomats in Riyadh have estimated that the Saudi government would spend up to $20 billion defending the riyal if necessary. 

 Asked whether he envisaged any more central bank intervention in the near future, Kazmi said some activity was always part of a regular monetary and exchange policy. 

 "They will come in enough to ward off any attacks on the currency, which as a central bank they should be doing," Kazmi said. 

 "We will continue to see these blips here and there, but there really doesn't seem to be any major fault in the currency as such." 

 The Saudi newspaper al-Eqtisadiah said the Saudi Arabian stock market also felt the weight of the currency, with its fall of 13.41 points or one percent to 1331.01 by Saturday's close mainly caused by the currency speculation.

title: ANALYSIS-Gulf  currencies  - To peg or not to peg?
text:
DUBAI, Feb 18 (Reuters) - Is a dollar peg a guarantee of stability for Gulf Arab currencies, or an indefensible anachronism that is bound to fall away eventually no matter how much money is poured into it? 

 Analysts in the Gulf Arab states are divided on the issue, and although most authorities say they are determined to defend their currencies right down to the wire, not everyone is convinced that will be enough. 

 The oil-rich Gulf Arab states, envied until recently for their seemingly unending wealth, are now labouring under sagging world oil prices which have hit their economies hard and forced them to adopt austerity budgets. 

 Their currencies, most of which are pegged to the U.S. dollar because it is the medium for pricing oil and so accounts for most of their exports, could be the next victims, some analysts say. 

 The Saudi riyal, which came under attack from speculators last year, is the first example many economists cite, adding that if the riyal falls all the other Gulf Arab currencies will tumble like so many dominos. 

 The Saudi riyal usually trades in a narrow band around its peg of 3.7500 to the dollar. Last August it came under pressure from foreign-based speculators who were betting on a devaluation as world oil prices declined. 

 Government sources said the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency (SAMA) or central bank pumped some $750 million into the market to bolster the currency. 

 "We have a very different situation now to what has happened in past years - you have got a chronic oversupply situation in the oil market and a troubled world economy, so it's not too encouraging really," said one Bahrain-based banker who asked not to be named. 

 But the Saudi Minister of Finance and National Economy, Ibrahim Abdel-Aziz al-Assaf, categorically ruled out any devaluation of the riyal late last year, saying there was no economic reason to take such a step. 

 Will the government be able to put its money where its mouth is if the riyal is targeted again? 

 "Looking at all the fundamentals and everything that goes into the currency, when the government here says they are not going to devalue I believe them," Kevin Taecker, chief economist at Saudi American Bank (SAMBA) , told Reuters. 

 The Saudi government traditionally defends the riyal through intervention rather than by increasing interest rates. Saudi Arabia last devalued its currency in 1986. 

 Diplomats in Riyadh said they estimated that the Saudi government would spend up to $20 billion in defence of the currency before eventually relenting. 

 They said devaluation could come within the next 18 months, while other bankers said it could occur as soon as the second half of this year. 

 But some economists felt the Gulf Arab states would not fall victim to the weaknesses exposed in Asian currencies. 

 "You have economies which are much less dependent on bank credit. They are not as highly geared on credit and are not as open to foreign investors," one Saudi-based economist said. 

 "There is also strong emphasis in Saudi Arabia to achieve higher levels of private sector growth and what is important in that is Saudi private capital... it is widely felt there is a lot of Saudi capital offshore and to attract that capital back it is important to maintain confidence in the peg," he said. 

 Bankers in Bahrain, the Gulf's main financial and banking hub, agreed but said this was exactly the danger that threatened regional currencies. 

 "It is largely a question of reputation and any loss of confidence in the riyal could cause locals to pull their money out of all the local currencies," one said. 

 But delinking from the dollar as a result of a forced devaluation does not have to be a negative step. 

 It could be a structured part of the economic diversification most Gulf Arab states are currently attempting. 

 Gulf News daily recently reported the United Arab Emirates' minister of communications and former minister of state for finance, Ahmed Humaid al-Tayer, saying if "we manage to delink our oil products from the dollar, we would be able to create a basket of currencies to avoid possible future political dangers. 

 "We would then have the choice to export our products in dollar, yen or other currencies and...avoid cases where one currency could be frozen. We can then export to countries dealing in euro with euro and in dollar with dollar." ((Gulf newsroom, +971 4 607 1222, fax +971 4 626982, dubai.newsroom@reuters.com)).
